body:
Understanding famine

A famine is a severe crisis in which large numbers of people cannot obtain enough food, resulting in widespread hunger, malnutrition and potentially high mortality.

Famines may develop after crop failures, but the failure of a harvest is not the only factor. Food prices, employment, household income, trade, transport and relief arrangements determine whether a shortage becomes a widespread human disaster.

Drought is a prolonged period of deficient rainfall or water availability.
Crop failure occurs when agricultural production falls severely.
Famine is a widespread crisis of access to sufficient food, often accompanied by starvation, disease and excess deaths.

A drought can cause a crop failure, and a crop failure can contribute to famine. However, these are not identical conditions. Not every drought produces famine, and famine can develop when vulnerable people lose the ability to purchase food even if some supplies remain available in markets.

Major famines during the colonial period

India experienced several severe famines during Company rule and the later period of direct British administration. Important examples occurred in Bengal, Odisha, northern India, southern India and western India.

PeriodPrincipal regionImportant historical fact
1769–1770BengalSevere famine during East India Company rule, associated with agricultural failure and an already distressed rural economy.
1837–1838Northern IndiaMajor famine affecting the North-Western Provinces and adjoining areas.
1866OdishaSevere famine, commonly known as the Na Anka famine; transport and relief difficulties aggravated the crisis.
1876–1878Southern and western IndiaGreat Famine affecting large areas, including Madras, Mysore and the Bombay region.
1896–1897Several Indian regionsWidespread famine affecting areas including the Central Provinces and parts of northern and western India.
1899–1900Western and central IndiaSevere famine affecting Gujarat, the Deccan and neighbouring regions following deficient monsoon rainfall.
1943BengalWartime famine involving a poor rice harvest, disrupted imports, high food prices and failures of distribution and relief.

The Bengal famine of 1770

The famine of 1770 occurred after the East India Company had obtained the Diwani of Bengal in 1765. As Diwan, the Company exercised important revenue-collection powers.

The Bengal countryside was already experiencing serious economic difficulties. The Company demanded substantial revenue, while cultivators and artisans faced financial pressure. Agricultural production and rural trade were under strain.

A severe famine then devastated Bengal. NCERT's Class 8 history textbook gives a traditional estimate of approximately 10 million deaths, representing about one-third of the affected population. This is a historical textbook estimate rather than an exact mortality count.

The disaster illustrates how agricultural failure combined with an impoverished rural economy could cause widespread mortality.

The Odisha famine of 1866

The Odisha famine of 1866, also known as the Na Anka famine, was a major disaster in eastern India.

Rainfall shortages and agricultural difficulties contributed to the crisis. Inadequate transport connections made it difficult to bring food supplies into affected areas quickly.

The experience highlighted the importance of communication, transport and timely relief in preventing deaths during food shortages.

After the famine, improving communications and transport became an important concern in discussions about famine prevention in Odisha.

The Great Famine of 1876–1878

The Great Famine of 1876–1878 severely affected southern and western India, including the Madras Presidency, Mysore and parts of the Bombay region.

Deficient monsoon rainfall caused severe agricultural failures in many affected areas. The crisis was intensified by poverty, the loss of employment and inadequate access to food and relief.

Deaths resulted not only from starvation but also from disease and the weakened health of malnourished people.

The severity of this famine contributed to later attempts to establish systematic principles of famine administration and relief.

The famines of 1896–1897 and 1899–1900

Widespread famine returned during 1896–1897, affecting several regions of British India.

Another major crisis followed during 1899–1900, when severe monsoon failure affected large parts of western and central India.

In Gujarat, the 1899–1900 disaster became particularly important in regional historical memory. It is commonly remembered as the Chhappaniya famine.

These late-19th-century famines demonstrated that an expanding railway system did not, by itself, eliminate food insecurity and famine mortality.

The Bengal famine of 1943

The Bengal famine of 1943 occurred during the Second World War. Its immediate circumstances differed from those of several earlier drought-related famines.

The crisis involved a poor rice harvest, the disruption of rice imports from Burma following Japanese occupation, wartime market disturbances and a sharp rise in rice prices.

Many vulnerable households became unable to purchase sufficient food. Serious failures in the timely distribution of supplies and relief contributed to the disaster.

The famine caused extensive deaths and suffering, followed by further disease-related mortality.

Do not assign a single cause to every colonial famine. Drought and crop failure were central to several major famines, while wartime supply disruption, price inflation and failures of distribution were particularly important in Bengal in 1943.

Prelims focus

  • 1770: Great Bengal famine during East India Company rule.
  • 1866: Na Anka famine in Odisha.
  • 1876–1878: Great Famine affecting southern and western India.
  • 1896–1897: Widespread famine across several Indian regions.
  • 1899–1900: Severe famine in Gujarat and western India.
  • 1943: Bengal famine during the Second World War.
  • Trap: Drought, crop failure and famine are related but distinct concepts.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 3, Ruling the Countryside, printed p. 27, 2020–21 printing; British Library, Indian Famine (Strachey) Commission, 1880, archival reference IOR/L/PARL/2/173/1, historical famine records; Odisha Review, August 2009, The Coast Canal in Orissa During the Colonial Era, section on the famine of 1866; Government of Bombay, Report on the Administration of the Bombay Presidency for 1899–1900, Summary, 1901; Government of India, Famine Inquiry Commission, Report on Bengal, 1945, Chapter XI, General Conclusions and Observations, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Major Famines in Colonial India: Chronology, Regions and Historical Context

body:
Why did food shortages become famines?

The severity of a famine depends on both the availability of food and people's ability to obtain it. Colonial Indian famines often developed when agricultural shocks occurred in communities already weakened by poverty, debt and limited access to alternative sources of income.

1. Failure of monsoon rainfall

Much of Indian agriculture depended on seasonal rainfall. When monsoon rains failed, farmers could lose their crops and income. Shortages of fodder also threatened cattle, which were essential for cultivation, transport and rural livelihoods.

Repeated rainfall failures could be especially destructive because households might exhaust their savings and food reserves during an earlier bad season.

2. Poverty and loss of purchasing power

A household's purchasing power is its ability to buy goods and services with the income and resources available to it.

During a food shortage, grain prices may rise sharply. At the same time, agricultural labourers may lose wages because farmers no longer require as much labour. Cultivators may lose their harvests and the income they expected from selling crops.

A family can therefore face a double difficulty: food becomes more expensive while its income falls.

How a food shortage becomes a household crisis

If grain is available in a town market but a labourer has lost employment and cannot afford the higher price, the existence of that grain does not protect the labourer from hunger. Food availability and the ability to purchase food are different conditions.

3. Revenue demands, debt and commercial agriculture

Colonial land revenue arrangements often placed substantial financial pressure on cultivators. When harvests failed, farmers could struggle to meet revenue, rent and debt obligations.

Some households borrowed from moneylenders, sold livestock or disposed of other productive assets to survive. These measures could reduce their ability to recover after the crisis.

The commercialisation of agriculture also increased dependence on cash income and market conditions. However, commercial cultivation alone did not automatically cause famine; the danger became greater when households lacked adequate food reserves, income or other means of obtaining food.

4. Transport and administrative difficulties

Food supplies could be available in one region while another experienced acute shortages. Poor roads, inadequate connections and delayed transport could prevent supplies from reaching affected communities.

Failures of administration could aggravate the problem when the authorities delayed identifying distress, moving supplies or providing assistance.

5. Disease and inadequate public health

Famine conditions weakened people's health. Malnutrition reduced resistance to infection, while migration and overcrowding could increase exposure to disease.

Consequently, famine mortality could include deaths caused by disease as well as direct starvation.

The relationship between these causes

A failed harvest did not have exactly the same effect on every household. A family with savings, stored grain or another source of income might survive a poor harvest. An agricultural labourer without work, savings or food reserves could face severe hunger much sooner.

This distinction helps explain why drought and famine were related but not inevitable consequences of one another.

Colonial famine relief measures

Relief policies changed during British rule. After severe famines, the colonial administration increasingly developed procedures for identifying distress and providing assistance.

Public relief works

Affected people who were able to work could be employed on public works, such as road construction or other approved projects, in return for wages or food.

The purpose was to provide income through which labourers could obtain food. However, low wages and demanding work conditions sometimes reduced the effectiveness of this assistance.

Gratuitous relief

Gratuitous relief meant assistance provided without requiring labour in return. It was particularly important for people unable to work, including severely weakened individuals and other destitute persons.

Food movement and distribution

Relief could also involve moving grain from areas with adequate supplies to famine-affected areas and arranging access to that food.

Railway connections could help with transport, but arrangements for distribution remained essential.

Other protective measures

Other measures included land revenue suspension or remission in particular circumstances, irrigation improvements, agricultural assistance and efforts to monitor changing crop and market conditions.

These measures were not applied uniformly or effectively in every famine.

Famine Commissions and Famine Codes

After the Great Famine of 1876–1878, the British Indian government appointed a major Famine Commission under Richard Strachey.

The Commission's report was submitted in 1880. It examined famine relief and recommended a more systematic administrative response.

Its recommendations influenced the development of provincial Famine Codes during the 1880s, including a model code developed in 1883.

Famine Codes were administrative guidelines intended to help provincial authorities recognise food distress, organise relief works and provide assistance to affected populations.

Further famine inquiries followed the major crises of the late 19th century, including reports in 1898 and 1901.

The development of Famine Codes represented an attempt to organise relief more systematically. It did not mean that famine deaths immediately ceased or that every administration responded adequately.

Gujarat connection: the Chhappaniya famine

The famine of 1899–1900 is remembered in Gujarat as the Chhappaniya famine, also commonly called Chhappaniyo Dukal.

The name is associated with Vikram Samvat 1956, corresponding to the period of the severe famine of 1899–1900.

Areas affected

The Bombay Presidency's contemporary administrative report identifies widespread famine distress in western India. In the Gujarat region, affected districts included Ahmedabad, Kaira (Kheda), the Panch Mahals and Broach (Bharuch), together with a large part of Surat district.

Principal causes

The monsoon failed severely in many areas, causing major losses of agricultural production. The shortage of fodder also affected cattle, while rising food prices and falling incomes increased hardship for rural households.

Relief measures in Gujarat

The Bombay Presidency's report for 1899–1900 records that authorities began test relief works in affected areas during August 1899. Regular relief works were opened in several districts by the end of October.

Gratuitous village relief was also provided for people unable to work. Poor-house relief for destitute persons began in Kaira during October and was subsequently extended.

These records show that relief arrangements existed, but they do not establish that assistance reached every affected person or prevented widespread suffering.

Effects on the population

The famine caused severe hunger, deaths, livestock losses and disruption of agricultural livelihoods. Families also faced indebtedness, migration and the loss of productive resources.

The Chhappaniya famine is therefore an important regional example of the combined effects of monsoon failure, rural poverty, food shortages and the limitations of colonial relief.

Prelims focus

  • 1880: Report of the Famine Commission under Richard Strachey.
  • 1883: Model Famine Code developed as part of systematic famine relief arrangements.
  • Public relief works provided employment-based assistance.
  • Gratuitous relief assisted people unable to work.
  • 1899–1900: Chhappaniya famine in Gujarat.
  • The name Chhappaniya is associated with Vikram Samvat 1956.
  • Trap: Relief works required labour, while gratuitous relief did not.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 1, printed pp. 10–13; British Library, Indian Famine (Strachey) Commission, Report of 1880, archival reference IOR/L/PARL/2/173/1; British Library, Report of Famine Commission, archival reference IOR/L/PARL/2/174, Parts I and II; Government of Bombay, Report on the Administration of the Bombay Presidency for the Year 1899–1900, published 1901, Summary, p. iii, British Library India Office Records IOR/V/10/311, accessible through Qatar Digital Library, consulted 20 November 2026; Report of the Indian Famine Commission 1901, Government of India, NITI Aayog Digital Library catalogue; Drought and Famine in India, 1870–2016, Geophysical Research Letters, 2019, section on the 1899–1900 famine.]
